utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. What is the number of the case, please? The case number on our docket.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This is IT-98-33-I, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) For the time being, please be seated, Mr. Krstic. Thank you. First of all, I would like to have the representatives for both of the parties. First, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Brenda Hollis, and along with my colleagues Mr. Peter McCloskey and Ms. Ann Sutherland. We appear on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Let me turn to Defence counsel for Mr. Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President and distinguished members of the Tribunal, my name is Nenad Petrusic, a lawyer from Belgrade, a member of the Lawyers' Chamber and I have been chosen to defend General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Today's hearing is an initial appearance which is carried pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in effect of International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and this always follows the arrest of an accused. In this case, the accused, Mr. Krstic, is now going to rise and tell us his name, his given name, his place and date of birth, his profession, and his domicile up to the point of his arrest. Please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) My name is General Lieutenant-Colonel Radislav. I am the commander of the 5th Corps of the army of the Republika Srpska. I was born on the 15th of February, 1948 in Vlasenica, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before I was arrested, I performed the -- my duties in Sokolac and my family lives in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. You may be seated for the time being. The interpretation said General Colonel. Could you explain that to me, please? Are you a General or are you a Colonel in the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am Lieutenant General of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. You may be seated for the time being. Let me remind you that further to the text in effect at the International Criminal Tribunal, I had read some relevant passages from the Statute, and will ask the registrar to read the relevant passages from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like to recall that further to the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal, specifically Articles 21 and 22, all persons against whom indictments have been confirmed, which is the case in here, and further to an order for a warrant of arrest which is issued by the International Criminal Tribunal to arrest, and the accused must be informed of the accusations against that person and then to be transferred to the International Criminal Tribunal, which is the case today. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber must read the indictment, and to be sure that the rights of the accused have been respected, to confirm that the accused understood the contents of the indictment, and ask him to plead guilty or not guilty, and the Trial Chamber will then set the date for the trial. There are other relevant passages relating to the rights of the accused. That is Article 21(1), (2), (3), (4); the person shall be informed of the charges against him, informed promptly and in detail, in a language which he understands, of the nature and cause of the charge against him, to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and communicate with counsel of his own choosing, and to be tried, of course, without undue delay, to be tried in his presence, and if he does not have counsel, to be informed of his right to have counsel, and if he does not, the Tribunal will assign one to him. It is under those conditions that Mr. Petrusic -- Mr. Petrusic, excuse me for mispronouncing your name -- was appointed -- did the Registry appoint you, Mr. Petrusic, or was it the accused who appointed you? Please rise and tell us under which conditions you were appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, I was elected by General Krstic to act as his Defence counsel, and if we're talking about language, the official language of the Tribunal, and as you have mentioned that Rule, I would like to say a few words in that regard, if I may. If you will allow me to do so. You do? Thank you very much. I know that according to the Rules of the Tribunal, the official language used is English or French. I speak neither of these two languages, but I do hope that this Trial Chamber will allow me to use Serbian, the language that the accused uses, and all further correspondence and anything in writing, any written documents necessary and any briefs will be in one of the official languages of this Tribunal. So in that regard, there will be no difficulty in communicating, that is, between the Defence and the Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Turning to the Prosecutor, will that cause any problems, that is the fact that Defence counsel does not speak either of the two official languages of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the qualification that Defence counsel just announced, and that is that pleadings, and correspondence and other written submissions would be in one of the official languages of the Tribunal, it would seem that the only thing that would be only in the Serbian language would be presentations made in court or in other proceedings, and the Prosecution would have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Thank you. I think that there's no objection from my colleagues. Under those conditions we can continue with the hearing, provided for also in Rule 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Turning to the registrar, we'll ask him to read that Rule. Please read it slowly so the accused can understand what is being said in his own language.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Rule 62, initial appearance of the accused. "Upon the transfer of an accused to the seat of a Tribunal, the President shall forthwith assign the case to a Trial Chamber. The accused shall be brought before that Trial Chamber without delay, and shall be formally charged. The Trial Chamber shall: (i) satisfy itself that the right of the accused to counsel is respected; (ii) read or have the indictment read to the accused in a language the accused speaks and understands, and satisfy itself that the accused understands the indictment; (iii) call upon the accused to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count; should the accused fail to do so, enter a plea of not guilty on the accused's behalf; (iv) in case of a plea of not guilty, instruct the registrar to set a date for trial; (v) in case of a plea of guilty, act in accordance with Rule 62 bis; (vi) instruct the registrar to set such other dates as appropriate."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. Of course, we will read Rule 62 bis only depending upon the plea entered by General Petrusic. I still don't understand if he's a General or Colonel, because his Defence counsel gives him the rank of General, he himself says Colonel. All right. Let's move on. All right. General Krstic. Thank you. We are now going to move to reading the indictment and this is how we will proceed. The indictment will be read by the registrar, and when the charges are read, I will ask the accused if he pleads guilty or not guilty. First of all, I would like to be sure, by asking Mr. Petrusic, whether as soon as the accused arrived in the detention centre that the indictment was given to the accused and that he understood the contents of that indictment. Did he, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, in the course of yesterday I spent 4 hours talking to my defendant. General Krstic has received the indictment, he has understood the indictment, so that at today's hearing he will be pleading on all the counts contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. The Prosecutor, to whom I will give the floor, has informed the Trial Chamber that the indictment that had been issued, among other things, against General Krstic had been subject to an order for non-disclosure from one of my colleagues who had confirmed it. This order for non-disclosure might also involve other people indicted in this indictment and that they be confirmed by the Judges as well. I give the floor to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we would remind you of the existing order that was issued by the confirming Judge pursuant to Rule 53, and we would ask that you confirm the ongoing nature of that order as to any other co-accused that may exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are there any comments from the Defence, Mr. Petrusic, while the Judges deliberate quickly at the bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. Thank you. Let me consult with my colleagues. Thank you to my colleagues. The Trial Chamber, this morning, confirms that referring to exceptional circumstances as covered by Rule 53(A) says, "In exceptional circumstances, a Judge or a Trial Chamber may, in the interests of justice, order the non-disclosure to the public of any documents or information until further order." We can also, pursuant to Rule 53(C), "In consultation with the Prosecutor, also order that there be no disclosure of an indictment, or part thereof, or have all or any part of any particular document or information. The Judges note that there is no objection from the Defence, and that under those conditions the registrar is now going to read the indictment against Mr. Krstic, but only as regards the relevant parts for the accused in this courtroom today. Lastly, let me remind Mr. Krstic that when I tell him to rise he will rise, and then the charge or charges will be read. At that point I will ask you whether you intend to plead guilty or not guilty. After that, we will, in a public session, organise the proceedings that will follow this hearing, which should lead to the trial. If there are no other comments, I will ask the registrar to rise and to read the indictment against -- excuse me, Mr. Petrusic. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I apologise to Your Honours and members of the Trial Chamber, but, Mr. President, when the indictment has been read out and when General Krstic pleads as to whether he is guilty or not guilty, that he be allowed, because of serious injuries, and I'll say a little more about that later on, may he remain seated, because if he has to get up, it will be difficult for him and I beg the Court's indulgence in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. The accused may remain seated when he's asked to plead guilty or not guilty. Now, turning to the registrar, would you please read the indictment against the accused this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This is IT-98-33-I the Prosecutor against Radislav Krstic. Indictment: The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the Tribunal, charges Radislav Krstic with genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war as set together below. Background: After armed conflict erupted in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the spring of 1992, Bosnian Serb military and paramilitary forces occupied cities, towns and villages in the eastern part of the country and participated in an ethnic cleansing campaign which resulted in an exodus of Bosnian Muslim civilians to enclaves in Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa. On 16 April, 1993, the Security Council of the United Nations, acting pursuant to Chapter VII of its Charter, adopted Resolution 819, in which it demanded that all parties to the conflict in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina treat Srebrenica and its surroundings as a safe area, which was to be free from any armed attack or any other hostile act. On or about 6 July, 1995, units of the Drina Corps of the Bosnia Serb army, the VRS, shelled Srebrenica and attacked Dutch-manned United Nations observation posts which were located in the safe area. The Drina Corps attack on the Srebrenica safe area continued through 11 July, 1995, when forces from the Drina Wolves, the Bratunac Brigade and other units of the VRS entered Srebrenica. The Bosnian Muslim men, women and children who were in Srebrenica after the beginning of the VRS attack took two courses of action. Several thousand women, children, and some mostly elderly men fled to the UN compound in Potocari, located within the safe area of Srebrenica, where they sought the protection of the Dutch battalion. The Bosnian Muslim civilians remained in and around Potocari from 11 July until 13 July, 1995, when they were evacuated by buses and trucks under the control of the VRS. A second group of approximately 15,000 Bosnian Muslim men, with some women and children, gathered at Susnjari village near Srebrenica during the evening of 11 July, 1995, and fled, in a huge column, through the woods towards Tuzla. Approximately one-third of this group consisted of armed Bosnian Muslim military personnel. The rest were unarmed military personnel and civilians. On or about 12 July, 1995, Ratko Mladic and Radislav Krstic, as well as other VRS and Bosnian Serb civilian representatives, met in the motel Fontana in Bratunac with Dutch military officers and representatives of the Bosnian Muslim refugees from Potocari. At this meeting, Ratko Mladic explained to the group that he would supervise the evacuation of refugees from Potocari and wanted to see all the Bosnian Muslim men between approximately the ages of 16 and 60 to screen for possible war criminals. On or about 12 July, 1995, in the presence of Ratko Mladic and Radislav Krstic, approximately 50 to 60 buses and trucks arrived at the military compound in Potocari. Shortly after the arrival of these vehicles, the deportation process of Bosnian Muslim refugees started. As Bosnian Muslim women, children and men started to board the buses and trucks, Bosnian Serb military personnel separated the men from the women and children, and detained the men in and around Potocari. Between the evening of 11 July 1995 and the morning of 12 July 1995, the Bosnian Muslims who had gathered in Susnjari formed a huge column and began their trek through the woods towards Tuzla. Bosnian Serb forces supported by armoured personnel carriers, tanks, anti-aircraft guns and artillery, positioned themselves along the Bratunac-Milici road in an attempt to intercept the column. Some of the armed members of the retreating column of Bosnian Muslims engaged in combat with the Bosnian Serb forces. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims from the retreating column were captured by or surrendered to Bosnian Serb military forces under the command and control of Ratko Mladic and Radislav Krstic. Between 11 July 1995 and 18 July 1995, VRS forces under the command and control of Ratko Mladic and Radislav Krstic participated in numerous incidents of opportunistic killings of Bosnian Muslim men shortly after they had been captured, as well as systematic summary executions of Bosnian Muslim men who were initially detained and then transported to various execution sites throughout the territory under the control of the VRS Drina Corps. The VRS forces under the command and control of Ratko Mladic and Radislav Krstic executed thousands of Bosnian Muslim men. Between 10 July 1995 and 18 July 1995, the VRS forces under the command and control of Ratko Mladic and Radislav Krstic either expelled or killed most of the members of the Bosnian Muslim population of the Srebrenica enclave. As a result of these actions, the VRS forces virtually eliminated the presence of any Bosnian Muslims in the Srebrenica enclave area, thus continuing an ethnic cleansing campaign which had begun in the spring of 1992. The Accused. Radislav Krstic was a Lieutenant Colonel in the JNA before the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Krstic served as commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, which was first a component of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps but was later transferred to the Drina Corps in 1992. He continued to serve as the commander of the brigade until late 1994. From January 1995 through 14 July 1995, he was Chief of Staff, Deputy Commander of the VRS Drina Corps. He was promoted to the rank of General-Major in June of 1995. On or before 14 July 1995, he assumed command of the Drina Corps. His assumption of command was publicly announced on 20 July 1995. In April 1998 he was promoted to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel General and is currently the commander of the VRS 5th Corps in Sokolac. Superior Authority. When the Srebrenica operation began on or about 6 July 1995, Radislav Krstic held the rank of General Major with the position of Chief of Staff, Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps. As Chief of Staff Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps, Radislav Krstic was responsible for directing the activities of the Corps staff. He was responsible for monitoring the activities of all units and activities within the Corps zone of responsibility, and also act as adviser to his Corps Commander. As Chief of Staff he was concurrently the Corps Deputy Commander, empowered to give orders on behalf of the Commander in his absence, and to give supplementing orders to insure implementation of the Commander's orders. When Radislav Krstic became the Commander of the Drina Corps on or before 14 July 1995, his responsibilities increased to include planning and directing the activities of all subordinate units in his zone of responsibility and monitoring their activities to insure his orders were implemented. General Allegations. At all times relevant to this indictment a state of armed conflict existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At all relevant times Radislav Krstic was required to abide by the laws or customs governing the conduct of war. All acts and omissions charged as crimes against humanity were part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against the Bosnian Muslim civilian population of Srebrenica and its surroundings. Radislav Krstic is individually responsible for the crimes alleged against him in this indictment pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal statute. Individual criminal responsibility includes committing, planning, instigating, ordering or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation or execution of any crimes referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the Tribunal Statute. Radislav Krstic is also, or alternatively, criminally responsible as a commander for the acts of his subordinates pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Tribunal Statute. Such criminal responsibility is the responsibility of a superior for the acts of his subordinates if he knew or had reason to know that his subordinate was about to commit such acts or had done so and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof. The general allegations contained in paragraphs 14 through 18 are realleged and incorporated into each of the charges set forth below. Charges. Counts 1 and 2: Genocide. Complicity to commit genocide. Between about July 1995 and 1 November 1995, Radislav Krstic, intending to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim people as a national, ethnical or religious group. (a) killed members of the group, and (b) caused serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group. Between about 11 July 1995 and 1 November 1995, Radislav Krstic planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of the opportunistic killings of captured Bosnian Muslim men from the Srebrenica safe area by VRS military personnel. Between about 11 July 1995 and 1 November 1995, Radislav Krstic planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of a planned and organised mass execution of thousands of captured Bosnian Muslim men from the Srebrenica safe area. The wide scale and organised killing of Bosnian Muslim men which occurred in several different locations in and around the Srebrenica enclave from 11 July 1995 until 18 July 1995 included: Potocari: Between 12 July 1995 and 13 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, summarily executed Bosnian Muslim men at diverse locations around the UN compound at Potocari where the Bosnian Muslim men had taken refuge. Kravica: On or about 13 July 1995, VRS soldiers, under the command of Radislav Krstic, summarily executed hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men who had been imprisoned in a large warehouse in the village of Kravica. The VRS soldiers used automatic weapons, hand grenades and other weaponry to kill the Bosnian Muslims inside the warehouse. Bratunac: Between 12 July 1995 and 14 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported many of the Bosnian Muslims who had been detained in Potocari or captured along the Bratunac-Milici road to locations in and around Bratunac where they were held in schools, buildings and vehicles parked along the road. Between 12 July 1995 and 15 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, participated in numerous opportunistic killings of the detained Bosnian Muslim men at various locations throughout Bratunac. Tisca: On or about 12 July 1995 and 13 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported the Bosnian Muslim women and children who had been separated from male members of their families in Potocari to an area near Tisca village. Most of the Bosnian Muslim women and children driven to Tisca were permitted to cross into Bosnian Muslim territory. However, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, identified and separated Bosnian Muslim men and some Bosnian Muslim women. On or about 12 July 1995 and 13 July 1995, the VRS military personnel forced the Bosnian Muslim men and women to walk to a nearby school where they were taunted and assaulted by VRS soldiers. On or about 13 July 1995 and 14 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, loaded 25 Bosnian Muslim men onto a truck, drove them to an isolated pasture and summarily executed them. Orahovac, near Lazete, on or about 14 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men from in and around Bratunac to the Grbavci School complex near Orahovac. On 14 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, summarily executed Bosnian Muslim men in and around the school. That same day the VRS military personnel transported the Bosnian Muslim men, many of whom were blindfolded, from the Grbavci school to the nearby village of Orahovac. Once there, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, ordered the Bosnian Muslim men off the trucks and executed them. Hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men were killed. On or about 14 and 15 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, used heavy equipment to bury the victims in mass graves at the execution site while the executions continued. The dam near Petkovci: On or about 14 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men from detention sites in Bratunac to the school at Petkovci. On 14 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, summarily executed Bosnian Muslims in and around this school. On or about the evening of 14 July 1995 and the early morning hours of 15 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported several hundred Bosnian Muslim men from the school at Petkovci to an area below the dam at Petkovci. These people were unloaded from vehicles, led in small groups to an open area and summarily executed by VRS military personnel under the command of Radislav Krstic. Cerska Valley: From on or about 14 July 1995 until about 21 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported over 100 Bosnian Muslim men to an area along a dirt road in the Cerska Valley, summarily executed them and covered them with dirt. Pilica: Between 14 and 16 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men from detention sites in Bratunac to the school at Pilica. VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, summarily executed many of the Bosnian Muslim men who were being detained at the Pilica school. Branjevo Farm: On or about 16 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men from the Pilica School to the Branjevo Farm. The Bosnian Muslim men were unloaded from buses, led in small groups to an open area and summarily executed with automatic weapons by VRS soldiers from the 10th Sabotage Detachment and other units. On or about 16 and 17 July 1995, the VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, using heavy equipment, buried hundreds of victims in a nearby mass grave. Pilica Cultural Centre: On or about 16 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, after participating in the Branjevo Farm executions, travelled a short distance to the village of Pilica. There, using automatic weapons and hand grenades, VRS military personnel executed approximately 500 Bosnian Muslim men inside the Pilica Cultural Centre. Kozluk: On or about 16 and 17 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, transported hundreds of Bosnian Muslim men to an isolated place near Kozluk and summarily executed them. On or about 18 July 1995, VRS military personnel, under the command of Radislav Krstic, using heavy equipment, buried the victims in a mass grave nearby. During and after the opportunistic killings and mass executions which occurred from 11 July until 18 July 1995, Radislav Krstic failed to investigate or punish any of his VRS subordinates who were responsible for the killings and executions. To the contrary, Radislav Krstic and units under his command participated in an organised and comprehensive effort to conceal and cover up the killings and executions by burying the bodies of the victims in isolated sites scattered throughout a wide area. When it became apparent that the International Community had learned of the killings and executions arising from the attack on the Srebrenica safe area, Radislav Krstic and units under his command participated in a second attempt to conceal the killings and executions by digging up the bodies from the initial mass graves and transferring them to secondary graves. VRS military personnel or their agents under the command of Radislav Krstic dug up the following graves and transferred the bodies to secondary sites. The Dam at Petkovci, Orahovac, Branjevo farm, Kozluk, Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, registrar. I want to ask you to stop for a moment. Let me turn to the accused. Mr. Krstic, please remain seated. The counts will now be read out, and at this point I'm going to ask you, as my colleagues do, to tell us whether you plead guilty or not guilty. First, let me ask you whether you feel well enough. Have you understood the indictment and did you learn of it when you reached the detention centre? Did you feel all right when you got there? Then I'm going to ask you to plead guilty or not guilty to each of the counts. You may remain seated when you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Do I have the right to speak? I have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter apologises. She heard it wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Do you hear me? Do you hear me? Do you hear me, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I can hear you very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just one moment to clarify the matter. Do you hear me now, Mr. Krstic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Did you hear the indictment? Were you connected properly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have heard the indictment, except for the last two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I ask the registrar to repeat the reading of those, please, that's paragraphs 24 and 25, and then tell us whether you hear. Do you hear? Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) During and after the opportunistic killings and mass executions which occurred from 11 July until 18 July, 1995, Radislav Krstic failed to investigate or punish any of his VRS subordinates who were responsible for the killings and executions. To the contrary, Radislav Krstic, and units under his command, participated in an organised and comprehensive effort to conceal and cover up the killings and executions by burying the bodies of the victims in isolated sites scattered throughout a wide area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You don't have to mention the paragraphs. Move on to the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) When it became apparent the international community had learn of the killings and executions arising from the attack on the Srebrenica safe area, Radislav Krstic, and units under his command, participated in a second attempt to conceal the killings and executions by digging up the bodies from the initial mass graves and transferring them to secondary graves. VRS military personnel or their agents, under the command of Radislav Krstic, dug up the following graves and transferred the bodies to secondary sites: The Dam at Petkovci, Orahovac, Branjevo Farm, Kozluk, Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Let me once again turn to the accused. You've now heard the indictment and you will tell us, please, whether you plead guilty or not guilty to each of the counts that the registrar will read from the indictment. I would, first of all, ask you to do the following: First, I would like to ask how you feel physically. Do you feel all right, other than the fatigue you feel in your leg? How do you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) As well as can be expected on the whole, but I am tired after the arrest, exhausted. At the detention centre, the people are very correct in their treatment of us all, and particularly to me myself. There has been no heating in the detention unit, however, for the past three days, and that is something which makes the circumstances impossible, and with regard to hygiene as well. In view of my injuries, I have no conditions for therapy for my leg, and for the care and attention of my health. So much for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I appreciate your having pointed this out. This will be indicated in our records to the registrar and to the head of the detention unit. I think it's absolutely important to have heating at this time of the year, and, of course, this applies to all of the accused, and more particularly to the accused and other treatment he should get. Let us move back to the indictment. Mr. Krstic. First of all, we'll ask the registrar to continue reading the indictment, and I'll ask you to plead guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Counts. By his respective acts and omissions described in paragraphs below, Radislav Krstic committed; Count 1: Genocide, punishable under Articles (4)(3)(a), and (7)(1) and (7)(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal; and alternatively: Count 2: Complicity to commit genocide, punishable under Articles (4)(3)(e), and (7)(1) and (7)(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. I'm turning to you, Mr. Krstic. I'm going to ask you, for these two counts which are listed alternatively, you are either accused of genocide or complicity to commit genocide by the Prosecutor. We will see the results of that during the trial. For the time being, we simply ask you to plead guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. This will be placed into the registrar's records. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Count 3, extermination. The Prosecutor re-alleges and reincorporates by reference the paragraphs below: By his respective acts and omissions described in the paragraphs below, Radislav Krstic committed: Count 3: Extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles (5)(b), and (7)(1) and (7)(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Krstic, do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Counts 4 and 5, murder. The Prosecutor re-alleges and refers to the allegations in the following paragraphs: By his respective acts and omissions described in the paragraphs below, Radislav Krstic committed: Count 4: Murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles (5)(a), and (7)(1) and (7)(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Krstic, do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Count 5: Murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Articles 3, and (7)(1) and (7)(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal, as recognised by Article (3)(1)(a) of the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Count 6, persecutions. The Prosecutor re-alleges and refers to the allegations contained in the following paragraphs: Beginning on 11 July, 1995 and continuing through 1 November, 1995, Radislav Krstic, committed, planned, instigated, ordered or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation or execution of a crime against humanity, that is the persecutions of Bosnian Muslim civilians on political, racial or religious grounds in Srebrenica and its surroundings. The crime of persecutions was perpetrated, executed and carried out by or through the following means: (a) the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians, including men, women, children and elderly persons; (b) the cruel and inhumane treatment of Bosnian Muslim civilians, including severe beatings; (c) the terrorising of Bosnian Muslim civilians; and (d) the destruction of personal property of Bosnian Muslims. By these acts or omissions, and the acts and omissions described in the above paragraphs, Radislav Krstic committed: Count 6: Persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article (5)(h), and (7)(1) and (7)(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Done this 30th day of October, 1998, at The Hague, The Netherlands, signed by the Deputy Prosecutor Graham Blewitt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) There is a final count. I would like to know as regards Count 6, the accused pleads guilty or not guilty? Persecutions on political --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. The Tribunal has noted that the accused has pleaded not guilty to all of the counts in the indictment, and at this point we will now, working with the -- consult with the Prosecutor and the Defence, to try to set the date for the trial. We are covered by Rule 62, and we must now organise the proceedings that will follow now in order to set, as quickly as possible, a date for the trial to begin. Madam Prosecutor, do you have several obligations which are covered by Rule 62 and following in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Have you satisfied all of your obligations which would allow us to set the date for the trial as quickly as possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to our obligation under Rule 66(A), on Friday we provided the supporting material relevant to this accused to the translation section of the registry for translation into the language of the accused. Today we are prepared to provide to the Defence counsel the English version of the supporting material that was provided for confirmation. We believe that there may be a videotape that would possibly qualify as a statement of the accused under Rule 66(a)(i). We have yet to view that videotape. As soon as we view it and determine that it does qualify under that section of the Rules, we will promptly provide a copy of that to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Petrusic, have you received all of the supporting material which is covered under Rule 66(a)(i)?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, during the course of the morning, about two hours ago, the only thing I did receive from the registrar are the Rules of the International Tribunal, and I also received the Statute. That is to say, the Rules and the Statute of this Tribunal. I did not receive any additional supporting material. Then, of course, the indictment was there too, the indictment that I was given by the accused yesterday when I saw him. So we did not receive any supporting materials. We cannot make any statements in this regard, and I hope that the Prosecutor shall provide these materials so that the Defence could also start collecting their materials. As far as the tape that the Prosecutor speaks of, I think it is too early for us to state our views on this, because I have my doubts as to whether this can be evidence or not, but we are going to state your views on this when the Prosecutor submits this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm not sure I quite understood that. All right. Madam Prosecutor, you have 30 days to disclose all of the supporting material with the indictment. You say you've already done that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have a copy for the accused in English. We do not have a copy in the accused's language, but we have that here and are prepared to provide that to the Defence Attorney at the conclusion of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Mr. Petrusic, you will receive them today. Does that mean, in your mind, Mrs. Hollis, that you do not need the 30-day time period? Do you feel that you've already satisfied your obligations under Rule 62(a)(i)? I'm saying that -- I'm talking about the supporting material. I would like to expedite the beginning of the trial. Aside from the video cassette, have you already or are you going to submit everything?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We're going to submit the supporting material relevant to this accused today at the conclusion of the proceedings, but they will be in English. As we read the current Rule, Your Honour, they have been provided in a language the accused understands. We have submitted them for translation, but we do not have the translated copies back as of today, in Serbian, and I'm not sure when the translation section will have that available for us, but we do have the English version here and we will serve that on the accused's counsel today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) All right. Let me turn to my colleagues. We could consider that the 30-day time limit today will suffice for the translations. You say that you have given the supporting material with the indictment not in a language that the accused understands, but that we can use the 30-day time period starting today, 7 December, that takes us to the 7th of January, so that all of the documents would have been translated. Mr. Petrusic, do you agree with that or can we speed up the translation process?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I agree with that proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. We can use that 30-day period. There's a second time period, Madam Prosecutor. About how many witnesses do you plan to call to this trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may take a moment to confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Do you have an approximate idea?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could give you a very rough estimate, and this would, of course, depend in part on what happens with our pre-trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would estimate somewhere in the vicinity of 50 to 70 witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. Let me turn to the Defence. Let me also tell the Defence that it will have a time period for filing any preliminary motions that it may care to do, once you have received all of the documents filed according to the appropriate Rules. If by the 7th of January you have received all of the statements, you will have to file your preliminary motions before the 7th of February, with that. Very well. From that point on, of course, we cannot say how long -- well, whether you're going to file any preliminary motions, that depends on you, not on the Judges. I don't know whether the Judges will be able to respond in the next few days. It will all depend on the legal substance of the preliminary motions, but can we today say that a trial around the end of March, the beginning of April will be possible,

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Prosecutor, Your Honour, yes, that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) On behalf of the Defence, it is very difficult, indeed, at this point in time to estimate when the trial could begin, and the Defence shall certainly resolve to all the rights vested in it in Rule 72 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and as the proceedings further evolve we shall also draw on Rule 65. So today, I did expect to see piles of documents provided by the Prosecutor, and we do not have a single shred of material from them. I repeat that it is unrealistic to set a time, whether it is going to be March or April, as you said, but the Defence cannot really say what period of time they would need to prepare their Defence, because we do not have a single shred of evidence from the Prosecutor so that we could speak about the date of the beginning of the trial. I hope you understand this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, we understand what you've just said, but I would like to say, on behalf of my colleagues, that the Prosecutor will be ready. That's the first observation, that the trial will begin as soon as possible. You have time periods which allow you to file a certain number of preliminary motions, and this is the right of the accused to file them and to raise them, but it will take time. It's your right, but that, of course, will postpone the date of the trial. The Judges must be prepared to move forward as quickly as possible as well. The Tribunal is very occupied at this time, but thanks to the fact that we have received some additional Judges, our schedule is reasonable and is possible to work with despite the workload of other cases. I don't think we can say anything further than that today. The Status Conferences will determine the legal follow-up to what has been said today, and the Trial Chamber has designated Judge Almiro Rodrigues as the pre-trial Judge. Let me remind that you the Status Conferences in cases, as a new procedure whose purpose is to accelerate the beginning of the trial itself, let me refer you, both the Prosecution and Defence, to 65 bis and 73 bis and ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Do you have any other comments you would like to make, Madam Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Petrusic, do you have any comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, since you have already asked about these comments, both the Prosecutor and for myself, allow me to make a comment. In all the trials before this Tribunal where military persons were indicted, the name of the accused was always preceded by his rank. I'm talking about Colonel Krsmanovic, General Djukic and now General Blaskic, too. However, in the indictment of General Krstic, his rank has not been mentioned, and I choose to interpret this as an accidental omission. I also wish to point out, with your permission, something that is really within the province of work of the Registry of this Tribunal. That is to say the truly seriously, imperilled health of General Krstic. A leg of his was amputated and there is atrophy of the muscle in the remaining part of the leg, and there is bleeding, too, and Mr. Krstic is rightly pointing to the threat of gangrene. The Registry of this Tribunal is going to deal with this problem; however, this is very serious and the consequences that may follow are very serious, and I wish this to be noted officially. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I believe that the registrar can tell us that the accused was already examined. This is ordinarily done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, he was examined when he arrived on the 3rd of December. At his arrival in The Hague, he was taken to the hospital where he was examined by a cardiologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Your comments have been noted, and if the accused needs any specific type of treatment, this is a possibility which we have run into before in this Tribunal, the proper treatment will be given to the accused. Before we finish our work, I would like to turn to my colleagues to ask if they have any comments and perhaps give the final word to the accused. Have you any statement you would like to make, General Krstic? Before you answer, Madam Prosecutor, you called the defendant what, General? Apparently he is a General. Do you call him Colonel General? What is your reaction to the Defence's comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our understanding is that the accused is a Lieutenant General in the Republika Srpska army. Indeed, he does hold a General rank, and it is the rank of Lieutenant General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, but what I want to know, in the indictment, the indictment that was read, he is referred to as Mr. Krstic. For my part, I have no problem to the military ranks being included, once they have been legitimately accepted and agreed to by the proper authorities. You call him Mr. Krstic, or shall we call him General Krstic? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would refer to him as General Krstic, if we refer to him other than by his last name, and in the description of the accused we do include his military rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Mr. Petrusic, I suppose that satisfies you. Before we give the final word to the accused, it will be noted here as being General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. President. I am satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And I note that the accused is also claiming his rank in the army of Republika Srpska, if we understood the comment. General Krstic, would you like to make any final statement, either seated or standing, before we finish our hearing this morning? Perhaps you have nothing to add; have you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. The Court stands adjourned.
